newsitem.title: UK: Labour says windfall tax should not hurt customers.
newsitem.headline: Labour says windfall tax should not hurt customers.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party said on Thursday that its proposed "windfall tax" on the profits of privatised utilities was legal and promised to ensure that customers would not be affected by the levy.
The party said it would introduce the tax, likely to hit companies such as water, gas and electricity producers, in its first budget if it wins power at the next election, due by May 22.
Finance spokesman Gordon Brown said experts believed it would be possible to prevent companies from trying to recoup the costs by raising prices to customers.
"I think we can take action to ensure that it should not affect them," he said in an interview with the Evening Standard newspaper.
But George Young, transport minister in the Conservative government, said Labour was planning to levy a "swingeing tax" on some of Britain's most successful privatised companies.
"Labour's windfall tax would also force up prices, hitting passengers on planes, trains, ferries and buses," Young said.
Labour said it would use the cash raised from the levy to fund a three billion pound "welfare-to-work" programme for the unemployed.
It has not specified which companies will be hit by the levy.
The Conservative government has over the past 18 years sold off major companies such as British Airways and British Telecom, as well as utilities such as British Gas and PowerGen.
Brown said three billion pounds might not be the limit on the tax.
"We may want to do more, but at a minimum the proposals will cost, over the life of a parliament, three billion pounds," he told the newspaper.
Speaking on BBC Radio, Brown said Labour had been told by legal advisers that there would be no obstacle to introducing the tax quickly and without fear of challenge in the courts.
"We want to move quickly on this," he said. "The budget will come within a few weeks of the general election if we are successful in persuading the country to vote for us."
Young called on Labour to clarify its tax plans and specify which companies would be affected.
"If Labour have had legal advice on their plans, then that must cover particular companies," he said.

The Conservative minister added that the windfall levy would hit shareholders in the firms, especially pensioners, who relied on income from pension funds which had invested heavily in such companies.
